utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would like to raise two preliminary matters, and the Defence one. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. First a very simple matter. General Smith has asked if he could have a hard copy of his statement as well as some blank paper to make a few notes, if necessary, regarding questions. I've shown this to Mr. Ivetic. He has no objection. So with the Court's permission, I would ask the usher to place this on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Permission is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Secondly, Your Honour, yesterday at transcript 7273, the Chamber expressed that it was still troubled by the discussion surrounding the legal status of the protocol attached to a memorandum from Akashi dated 16 August 1994 and now in evidence as D112. Lest any confusion take root, I want to direct the Chamber to Prosecution Exhibit P631 which is a second memo from Akashi which specifically references the 16 August memo by number, Z1256. In P631 [realtime transcript read in error "613"], Akashi makes a clear statement of the legal status of the protocol the Defence has suggested had been accepted and had legal effect: "The attached protocol in contrast is a Bosnian Serb proposal that was never accepted by us, the protocol was sent to us in error, and was forwarded to you without a full examination." Akashi attached to this correspondence an assessment of the document from the UNPROFOR senior legal advisor which unequivocally stated: "Draft that had been prepared and submitted by the Bosnian Serb negotiators but was found acceptable -- unacceptable by the UNPROFOR negotiators and was never signed. Accordingly, it cannot be regarded as having any legal standing." Your Honour, this fact is also corroborated by the evidence of RM163 at transcript page 6175, RM055 at transcript page 7225, and General Rose at transcript page 6976. Your Honours, it is the Prosecution's position that P613 is dispositive of the legal status of the protocol proposed by the Bosnian Serbs in D112. However, we stand ready to explore the matter further should the Chamber take a different view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- well, Mr. Groome, whether this resolves all the problems is still to be seen. But at least you have now pointed at what you consider to be the relevant sources for the Chamber to make an assessment on the legal status. Mainly, also documents which came months and months after the protocol apparently was drafted. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just correct the record. On page 2 at line 14 I'm recorded as having said "613," I intended "631." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I jotted down on my piece of paper. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just briefly to respond to the arguments presented by counsel, I wasn't aware we were at that stage of the proceedings, but I would ask Your Honours to keep an open mind and examine all the evidence as indeed I believe even the testimony of this witness who is coming today will be illustrative on the fact of the protocols and how they were viewed by those on the grouped on both sides on UNPROFOR and on the side of the combatants, the combatting parties. But I rise for another matter, Your Honours. As a preliminary matter to this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As a preliminary matter to this witness being brought in, it is my duty to rise and bring to your attention a matter relating to the list of exhibits for this witness. Your Honours have issued a guidance whereby the initial list of exhibits for a witness are to be given seven days in advance of their testimony. In this case, we did receive such a list and it was, indeed, a very lengthy list of documents, some three binders' worth once printed. Your Honours have also stated that upon proofing the list can be amended with a reasonable number of documents which arise during proofing. Here, the proofing of the witness was on the 8th of January, 2013. At least that is according to the information report which we have received. That information report which we received the 18th of January, 2013 was dated the 11th of the January, 2013, and did not list any new documents arising from the proofing. Now, just one day before the witness was scheduled to testify, that is, on the 22nd of January, and almost a full two weeks after the witness's proofing session, we all of a sudden receive notice of some seven new documents that are being added to the Prosecution list for this witness with no explanation of where they came from, and I have to say granted upon review we now note that four are extracted from existing documents that were on the list but three are completely new. Unless there was a new and undisclosed to us proofing of this witness, we do not know how and why these new documents arise just before the day that a witness of this complexity is scheduled to testify, especially since they were all on the Rule 65 ter list previously and apparently did not arise during proofing. I need to know, and the members of the Defence team need to know, for purposes of knowing how to best represent and protect the rights of our client, in light of Your Honours' previous guidance, and the established practice of the Prosecution to date, what exactly is the law of the case as to the addition of documents to the direct examination list for a witness? What are the methods of enforcement and what are the remedies? Because we still don't have a clear answer to these questions or a clear ruling from the Chamber on the degree of notice that our client and his Defence team are entitled to for Prosecution witnesses, even if this may be for future witnesses and not this particular witness. I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Groome, three entirely new documents, because that's the core of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Ivetic to tell us -- I'm unaware of three new documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By way of e-mail, January 22nd, 9.47 a.m., we received 65 ter numbers 2227M, 22270P, 22270S, 01691A, 01624A, 05258, 27625, and P38. It is my understanding that the last three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, yes. I asked for the three. But the last three ones are entirely new in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honours. I don't have the break down of the documents in front of me, but it's -- three of those documents are entirely new. I can tell from looking at them that the first four appear to be ones that were extracted from an existing -- existing audio recording that was on the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, more than a week before this witness testified the Defence was provided with a list, a very detailed list of the exhibits that would be used. With respect to 2270, over the course of the week we limited -- it's a set of intercepts. We limited the number of intercepts and we gave specific information about that. With respect to P38, that is an original UNPROFOR report that appears in 3535, 65 ter 3535. We -- Prosecution gave notice that we would also be using P38, which is the same as that, but that we would also be asking the witness to look at that. The other two, Your Honour, I would have to take a look in e-court. I believe they are intercepts, and I believe that we did give notice of them. I'm sorry, 5258 is a map of the Srebrenica area, and I can indicate now I will not use that with the exam. But it was simply a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And 2765 is an intercept that I will not be using today as well. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we have 27625 mentioned by Mr. Ivetic. Is that the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the same one, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I will not be using that today, Your Honour. I believe it was part of a larger collection of intercepts as well, but I'm not going to use that today, so I don't believe there is any exhibits that I'm using today that the Defence did not have more than a week's notice that I would use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, when did you receive those new documents, you said? Let me see. The 22nd, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I take it you immediately contacted the Prosecution, asked them, What are you doing now coming with entirely new documents isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, because it's happening with every witness. So I don't do that. I look at the documents and see whether it's a problem with this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, next time -- we're talking seven documents, some of them clearly linked to other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next time you're hereby invited, if you want to be -- raise these matters, with the weight, with the heaviness, you do it first one call to the Prosecution. Because here you say it happens with every witness. Here it apparently did not happen entirely with this witness. If you look at the map, and if it's just a map of the Srebrenica environment and the area, then, of course, before asking a ruling from the Chamber on what remedies, I would say, well, we have a map, which now, by the way, is not used and that, of course, confuses. That's clear. Mr. Groome, if you sent lists of documents you say you're not going to use, I think it is better not to do that, but perhaps you'd still have to make up your mind. Mr. Ivetic, if you look at it, give a call to Mr. Groome and say, What are you doing now? Because the first thing the Chamber would ask is what is the type of the document. If it is simply a map of Srebrenica area, then there may not be that much reason for the strong language you used. We move on. The Chamber will consider your request. If there's nothing else to be raised, then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smith. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Please be seated. When I address you as "Mr. Smith" without title and rank, it's not out of disrespect but for us witnesses of the truth are irrespective of titles and ranks. Mr. Groome, you may start your examination of the witness. Mr. Smith, you will first be examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to begin your testimony by stating your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My full name is Rupert Anthony Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Smith, it's important that the Chamber have an understanding of your military background, something which is covered in detail in paragraphs 3 to 5 of your statement which I will tender for admission in a few minutes. Can I ask you to simply, at this stage, state how long was your military career and what was the highest rank that you achieved?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I served for just under 40 years, and I was a full general in the British Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 28631 be brought to our screens. It is a statement of General Smith given on several different dates and signed on the 21st of September, 2009. General while your statement is being brought to our screens, can I ask you to tell us whether you ever served in Bosnia-Herzegovina and, if so, tell us in what capacity and during what period.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I served in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 for most of that year, from early January -- I'm sorry, late January to the end of the year, just before Christmas. And I was the commander of the UN forces with the title of commander UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My immediate military superior was General Janvier and the Force Commander in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: General Michael Rose had been my predecessor as commander UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Smith, we can see the document before you. Can I ask that you look at this first page and tell us whether you recognise any of the signatures in the bottom right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I recognise at least two of them; that is, mine and of a lady called Carolyn Edgerton underneath that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is the document that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The witness statement that was signed and made -- made by me and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we slow down slightly. You are both speaking the same language and therefore a short pause between question and answer and answer and question would be appreciated by our interpreters and transcriber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the signatures there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the same two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before testifying today, did you have an opportunity to read and review this statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to read it and review it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In that process, were two typographical errors identified?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Although I can't remember where they were in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to paragraph 62. On e-court, that is 15 in the original and 12 in B/C/S. The third line in that paragraph contains an 8-digit evidence reference number of a document you referred to in your statement. The first four digits of that number are incorrectly recorded in the statement as 0632, when, in fact, they should be 0362; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now go to paragraph 75. In e-court, this is 18 in the original, 14 in the translation. And more precisely, to the second line in that paragraph, which refers to a document ending in ERN number 9398, purportedly dated 28 March 1995. Have you now learned that the translation of this document you were shown had a typographical error and that the date of this document is, in fact, 26 March, and, hence, this should be considered in reading this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have learned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the Chamber were to consider your statement in conjunction with these two corrections, would it have an accurate record of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I were today to ask you questions similar to those you were asked in the taking of the statement, would you give the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, having established the foundational requirements necessary, the Prosecution, at this time, tenders 65 ter 28631 into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 ter as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence would at this time object to the tendering of this statement and would refer Your Honours to our filing of 1 January 2013, wherein we objected not only to the number of associated exhibits, 56, we objected to certain non-tendered associated exhibits being quoted from verbatim in the statement. We also objected to multiple associated exhibits that were not integral to the statement pursuant to Your Honours' rulings in prior instances with other witnesses, and we objected to some, I believe, 19 paragraphs containing improper expert opinion that had not been qualified under the appropriate criteria of Rule 94 bis. To my knowledge we have not received a decision on this motion, so we would suggest that pursuant to our objections that can be MFI'd until Your Honours reach a final determination as to these issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, anything -- the Chamber usually decides on admission at the end of the testimony and then also will consider the -- the associated exhibits and the non-associated exhibits. Apart from those used during the testimony. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to proceeding in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number assigned to the statement of the witness, 65 ter 28631.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will receive number P785, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, despite the fact that the statement is in evidence, may I summarise the evidence contained therein for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll hear the evidence and the questions anyhow, so, therefore, you may summarise it, although it should also be clear on the record that it's not yet admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A summary of the evidence of General Rupert Smith. General Rupert Smith was commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina from January 1995 until the end of the conflict. In this capacity, he held numerous meetings with Bosnian Serb political and military leaders, including Mladic, Karadzic, and Krajisnik. Based on this interaction as well as other observations, General Smith provides evidence about the nature and function of the VRS. His evidence addresses VRS interference with humanitarian assistance and the resupply of UN personnel, the taking of UN personnel hostage, events during 1995 related to Sarajevo, Srebrenica; in particular, the massacres in Srebrenica and the second shelling of Markale market. He provides evidence of his interaction and meetings with General Mladic and describes an occasion when he and the Secretary-General's Special Representative were shot at as they landed in Sarajevo airport and another occasion when his helicopter came under fire. General Smith also provides evidence of his meeting with General Mladic on the 15th of July, 1995. Your Honours, that concludes a brief summary of General Smith's evidence. Of course, should the Chamber admit his statement, it will be available to the public as well. May I proceed with some additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 23867 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, over the course of my examination of you here this morning, I will ask you to provide additional detail regarding portions of your statement, as well as to invite you to make observations on documentary evidence. We're calling up now 23867.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is not in e-court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. We'll investigate if there's a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was a mistake there. It is there now. If I could ask the Court Officer to try again. And could I ask that we go directly to page two in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, I would ask you to take a look at the document on the screen. It is an UNPROFOR report dated 14 February 1995, recording what occurred at a meeting between you and General Mladic on the same day. Did you have an opportunity to review this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was this your first meeting with Mladic? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure. It -- I think it was my second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to point 6 in the report. It is on e-court page 3 in both languages. And this is the portion of the report that is of greatest relevance to this case, and I want to read it to you: "Evacuation from enclaves, Mladic repeated his offer of an evacuation of 450 people, each from Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. This was a gesture of good faith, and the old, the young, and the women of university age would be selected. This is an offer which has been made previously to the Force Commander. We propose to tread carefully here, bearing in mind the pitfalls associated with this idea." Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber what the phrase "we propose to tread carefully here" referred to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There -- we were -- we were in -- there were three things that I think was behind that sentence. The first is that we, the UN, were a third party in this, and I wasn't about to make a set of agreements that I didn't have an understanding of the other parties' position in these matters. And frequently during the story of UNPROFOR in Bosnia, we, the UN, had found ourselves making agreements that we couldn't then discharge because the other party wouldn't agree with us in this triangular relationship. The second, was that there was a danger of us, if you like, conducting ethnic cleansing ourselves by moving people out of these enclaves and so on and so forth. And, thirdly, and perhaps, that you weren't sure that the -- the basis of the deal that the -- that necessarily you would get the return on -- that was being offered on us being able to take people out of an enclave or some other set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours at this time the Prosecution tenders 23867.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence as to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23867 receives number P786, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Smith, women of university age is a concept not -- I'm not familiar with. Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this distance, while I may have understood what that meant then, I'd be pressed to be sure of what we meant. I imagine young women in their 18-to-22 age group. But I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which would mean that women of -- well, let's say, anything between 25 and 50 would be excluded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now draw your attention to paragraph 35 of your statement, P785, marked for identification. This can be found in 9 of the original and 7 of the translation. In this paragraph you provide evidence about the inability of UNPROFOR to access the Srebrenica enclave. My particular question, in addition to what you have in this paragraph -- in this particular paragraph, is are you able to estimate the number of times you or your staff requested access to the UN safe area in Srebrenica and were denied such access?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It -- I certainly asked to be able to do this when I first -- I think I first met the Bosnian Serb leadership at Pale. And I know my staff were pursuing this request, and I would have thought that we'd -- it was probably raised two or three times in the first few weeks of my time in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you enumerate the reasons, if any, that you and your staff were given when you were denied access to the safe area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: From memory, they were -- it wasn't safe. You -- we couldn't secure your presence because the -- there were -- the Bosnians were attacking out of these enclaves and so forth. That it -- they couldn't provide escorts, or you were just not given a reason. You were just told, No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when you mentioned that it wasn't safe, can you be specific? It wasn't safe for who?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It wasn't safe, it was said, for me and my party. The Bosnian Serbs could not guarantee my security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In consideration of these repeated denials of access and the fact that permission was eventually provided by Mladic himself, did you understand Mladic to be personally controlling access to the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think it's speculation and I believe that Mr. Groome is testifying in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I certainly didn't mean to testify. I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, who did you understand to be personally controlling access to, if anyone, to the safe area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Access by me was being controlled by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 3822 be brought to our screens. It's a record of a meeting between Generals Smith and Mladic, held on 5 March 1995. The first page is simply a cover sheet, so could I ask that we go to e-court page 2 immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you are able to see the document, can I first ask you whether it is a document you had an opportunity to examine in preparation for giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 of your statement, you provide testimony of this 5 March 1995 meeting in Jahorina. Can I draw your attention to paragraph 3, and that's 3 in the original and in B/C/S, in particular, the first two sentences which read: "General Smith questioned General Mladic on the reason for the upsurge sniping attacks in Sarajevo. General Mladic cited recent Serb casualties from BiH attacks." Can you explain this particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The background is that we still have this Cessation of Hostilities Agreement in being, and the -- there had been a steady rise in incidents around Sarajevo and elsewhere, but this is considering the Sarajevo one. And I'm trying to understand the Serb position in the -- Bosnian Serb position in this rise of incidents, as to what it was behind them, we were not clear at that stage, the motivation of these attacks, although I was becoming clearer as the weeks went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did General Mladic acknowledge that his troops were responsible for an upsurge in sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He is explaining that -- he is saying they're reacting to the upsurge in the Bosnian sniping but, then, yes, they are involved as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he seem informed about the activity of snipers in -- in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He certainly understood that this was going on. This was no -- no surprise to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 39 of your statement, that's ten in the original, 8 in the B/C/S, you say: "He," referring to Mladic, "He threatened a complete blockade of all enclaves including Sarajevo if sanctions were not lifted. I took the threat seriously. He had the demonstrable ability to do what he had threatened." I would like you to further explain this last statement when you said that he had the demonstrable ability. What you did mean precisely?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, his forces controlled the route into these enclaves, and every convoy, every truck, had to be -- go through Bosnian Serb check-points. So that was one control. Secondly, the UN had in previous years accepted that UN convoys were searched, that convoys were -- you had to list what you were putting in the vehicles before the convoy was given clearance, if it was given clearance at all, and so all -- all of those controls, if you like, administrative controls, were in place as well. And then, finally, we, the UN, and the troop contributing nations had shown no interest in forcing a convoy through. So we were unlikely to fight our way through in order to get a convoy into, for example, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 3822 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3822 becomes Exhibit P787, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P787 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraphs 54 to 58 of your statement, you describe your meeting with Mladic in Vlasenica on the 7th of March. I would like to direct you to paragraph 57. It is 14 in the original, 11 in the translation, where you describe Mladic telling you that he had restricted the amount of food, medicine, and fuel for the enclaves, and your reply that an attack on the UN Safe Areas would risk a response by NATO. You then say: "This brought forward a tirade of threats of counteraction from Mladic." Can you tell us with as much detail as you recall the threats that General Mladic made as well as his demeanour when he made these threats?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember the threats in any great detail. They -- they were largely centred, as I recall, on British -- the threat was being made against British forces on the grounds, I understood, that I was a British officer, and that people would have their throats cut and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask now that we have 65 ter 1624 brought to our screens. Your Honours, the military notebook recovered from the Mladic home are already in evidence. In addition to these books a collection of audiotapes was also recovered from the same location. They're on the Prosecution list, based on an initial review which indicated many of them were likely recordings made by General Mladic of events relevant to the indictment. A more detailed analysis has taken place, and the Prosecution is now in the process of drafting a bar table. I will work with several of them today which relate to General Smith but will only, at this stage, ask that they be marked for identification. And if I -- I'm sorry, if it could be 1624A. I misspoke. General, when you can see 1624A on the screen before you, can I ask you to look at it and tell us whether it is a document that you had an opportunity to review in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Having read the transcript, did you recognise the subject matter being discussed in this tape?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you recognise the subject matter from?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I can -- he is talking about this meeting in Vlasenica. It appears to be a conversation about a day after the meeting. And he is explaining what he said to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: -- in the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention specifically to that, about three-quarters of the way down the page, we can see Mladic say: "I will cut Smith off. I won't give him any food until this can go in a normal way." Do you recall him threatening to impede the supply of food to UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh yes. The -- the -- at that point in the meeting in Vlasenica, there was this -- the whole argument, if you like, or point that he was making, was that we were supplying more than was absolutely necessary. They were under sanctions. We should be under sanctions. And that had been said as well at Jahorina some two days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page we can read the following: "Since you are English and threatening, and he said, I am the United Nations, then I'll take your Englishmen from Gorazde and in front of cameras cut one head off for each threat. Publicly. And I'll show it to CNN, and don't think that I won't do this." My first question is do you recall Mladic making threats along the lines of this to you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Although I suspect what reached me in translation wasn't necessarily quite as he is explaining it to -- in this telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what the phrase "Englishmen from Gorazde" refers to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There was British battalion in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No consultations, Mr. Mladic. You can write down whatever you want. Pass a note to counsel and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that 65 ter 1624 be marked for identification pending a written application to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to that procedure being followed for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. It's 1624A again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1624A receives number P788, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 of your statement, that's in 15 -- page 15 and page 12 respectively in e-court, you recount your flight into Sarajevo with Mr. Akashi and the Force Commander on the 12th of March and describe how it was hit by heavy machine-gun fire. Can I ask you to describe the plane, in particular the outer markings on the plane?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Ivetic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've received a note from my client asking for a break. I do not know the reasons since I'm not allowed to consult with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a -- your client can write down the reasons for which he wants a break and pass it onto you. Mr. Ivetic, I'm not amused by your physical expression of discontent with the Chamber's ruling. I would leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would take exception with Your Honour's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break in seven minutes. If there's any specific reason, Mr. Mladic can write a little note and we'll hear what the reasons are. Mr. Ivetic, I emphasise that this regime was imposed after repeated abuse by Mr. Mladic, and that is the reason why it is there. Nothing else. Mr. Smith, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The aircraft was a Russian YAK. It was the type of aeroplane. It was a small, we might call it a commuter jet. And it was run by Ukrainian organisation on contract to the United Nations, and the airplane was painted -- certainly had UN markings on and was, as I recall, painted white.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was notice given to -- to the parties to the conflict about the expected arrival of this flight?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been the standard procedure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have an air force? In other words, did any military aircraft belonging to the ABiH use Sarajevo airport if you know?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, they didn't have an air force, and no they didn't have aeroplanes flying into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 63, you say: "My recollection is that the incident was almost immediately protested and faced with this protest, Mladic agreed that it had been his people who had fired." By "people," did you intend -- was it intended that people were the troops under Mladic's control?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You had additional meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These little pauses, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You had additional meetings with Mladic after this event. Did he ever inform you of any disciplinary action he took with respect to the troops involved or describe an investigation he ordered into this event?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember him doing either of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraphs 78 to 96 of your statement records your evidence with respect to events in April 1995. Can I draw your attention to paragraph 79, that's 19 in the original, 15 in the translation of your statement, there you describe a private meeting you had with Dr. Karadzic on the 5th of April, 1995, at a hotel near Pale. The penultimate sentence in that paragraph reads: "I took the step of contacting Karadzic because at this stage General Mladic refused to ... speak with me on the telephone, and my letters to him requesting meetings went unanswered."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, your quote was not complete. You left out refused to meet or speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that you place this sentence in context and perhaps explain what you meant in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- I mean, I'm not sure I can expand on it. He wasn't communicating with me. The context of the -- of the -- the situation at that time was that the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement had more or less broken down by this stage. It was breaking down. The -- the -- we, the UN, were being seen increasingly as -- by the Bosnian Serbs as irrelevant, a nuisance in the way rather than anything that was going to be of use to them, and on top of that, there was a particular cause in that in the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, there was a -- a requirement for each side to place liaison officers with the UN, and the Bosnian Serbs had provided two liaison officers who were with the British headquarters at Sector South-west. But by the virtue of the agreement breaking down, this -- these arrangements were useless and the -- the two liaison officers were sitting in the headquarters at Gornji Vakuf and were an embarrassment as much to us -- to themselves as they were to the UN. And Mladic knew I wanted to get them back to the -- but he wasn't going to relieve me of this embarrassment and didn't want to talk to me, and subsequently I sent them back, which became a cause for another round of -- of disagreements between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be guided by the Chamber whether there's time for one more question or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have one minute left. So please proceed, with one last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Paragraph 94 of your statement, and that's at 23 in the original, 18 translation, it describes an incident on 21st of April during which the US and German members of the contact group were effectively detained by the Bosnian Serb army at Sarajevo airport. You go on to assert that you believe the decision to do this was a military one in which Mladic was personally involved. My question is: Can you tell us why you came to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Because it was -- Mladic's people who were -- had, in effect, created the situation, and it was with them that we were having to negotiate. And every time you got Professor Koljevic moving towards a solution to this problem, then he just came up against an inability to persuade Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no follow-up to that particular answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Groome. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask that 65 ter 5518 be brought to our screens. It's an order from the VRS Main Staff, issued on 27 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, your statement, at paragraphs 118 and following, addresses NATO air-strikes at the end of May 1995 and the taking of UN personnel as hostages. When the English version of this order comes to the screen before you, could I ask you, have you had a chance to review this document prior to today?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The document states "I hereby order," and then sets out 9 paragraphs of specific orders. The first directs that captured UNPROFOR staff be placed "at the warehouses, in the areas of command posts, firing positions, and other potential targets that may come under the air-strike." The second paragraph sets out the specific number of hostages to be sent to four different corps. What, if anything, does this document indicate about the level at which the decision to use UNPROFOR personnel as human shields was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object. Calls for speculation for an expert opinion for which this witness has not been qualified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question. The witness may answer the question. The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall the question?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, thank you. It shows that it's from the Main Staff, that they're controlling this, and because I've seen the document, you showed it to me, it is signed by Mladic, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we advance to the second page of the document just to be sure there's no mistake.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm wrong. By the chief of -- the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 5518 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the document being tendered in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5518 becomes Exhibit P789, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P789 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Ivetic, may I take it when your microphone was not activated that you had said what you wanted the Chamber to listen to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I believe I had activated it after to say I had no objection to it being tendered in that manner, as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 27615 be brought to our screens. It is an intercept dated 26 May 1995 at 1105 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, in your statement beginning at paragraph 123 you describe three long telephone conversations with Mladic. In preparation for your evidence, did you have an opportunity to review the transcript which is now being brought to our screen, which purports to be a record of one of these conversations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you read it in -- when you --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect the conversation between you both on the 26th of May 1995 as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, as best as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the transcript, we can see midway down the page you say the following: "I must remind you that using these prisoners as a human shield is against the Geneva Convention. Those other" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I again ask everyone to slow down and to make these pauses as the court reporter asks us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll pick it up from "after Geneva Convention." "... those other armies and the UN colours represents the violation of a protocol and the threat to kill, not only does it violate the Geneva Convention but also, besides the shelling of Tuzla, ... Tuzla is another violation ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In this passage, you are informing General Mladic that his conduct is a violation of international law. Did you form an impression during your conversation whether or not he appreciated this fact?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think he appreciated me telling him this. Whether he understood what I had said, I think he probably did, but I'm not -- my impression at the time was that that wasn't very important to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 27613 be now be brought to our screens. It is an intercept dated 26 May at 1446 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, once again, once you are able to see the document on your screen, can you tell us whether it's one you've had an opportunity to review in preparation for your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And after having reviewed it, does it accurately reflect the conversation between yourself and General Mladic on the 26th of May as best as you're able to recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About midway down the page, we can see Mladic refer to something called a "HRIPE-1." Do you recall him saying something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. My particular memory is that I didn't understand it, and we -- it -- we later learnt that it meant something like death rattle. Or -- that's what we understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You go on to say: "The air-strikes took place because of those decisions you yourself took personally." Can you tell us what decisions you are referring to and upon what basis did you believe General Mladic took them personally?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This is the -- can you give me the line? I'm just looking for where I go on to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's further down. I think it's in the lower half. Let me see ... Sorry, it's about midway.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you see? It says: "The camera will tell him," then it has S, "as I explained to you." Just under HRIPE.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. My -- I -- what I think I'm explaining there or trying to get across to him is that it is he that has taken the decisions not -- well, first, to remove weapons from the weapon control points or to use the weapons in the weapon control points, and then to -- and to -- and then when the ultimatum had been given to stop doing that and to put them back into weapon control points, this was ignored. If the -- he had not made the decision to use the weapons against the exclusion zone regime and had then accepted the ultimatum, then none of the air-strikes would have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 27615 and 27613 as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would object based upon the lack of showing us the provenance of these documents and how they were prepared and, in particular, if there is any audio or video material upon which they are based. This witness has given his evidence so I would suggest, therefore, that these be marked for identification pending resolution of those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution submits -- or I can first make the representation that there are no audiotapes. There it's the -- the transcript that we have. And I submit that adequate foundation has been laid before you. You have the person who was one party to the telephone conversation has reviewed this and says that they accurately reflect the conversation as best as he can recall. So I believe there is sufficient foundation for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any need for further comments? Especially on the presence of the witness who testified to the accuracy of these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. He has testified as to portions that have been presented to him. Whether this is the entirety of the conversation or not, I don't know. And therefore it is important to have the individuals who created this document to identify how they took the document, whether in fact it is a true and complete copy or if it is an extract, I don't know. All I have is a piece of paper with no heading indicating words from -- with no signatures, with no seals, that purports to be a conversation. I mean, this could have been printed up on a computer, and if portions of it are consistent with the witness's memory, that doesn't mean that the entirety is consistent with the witness's memory. If we're going to be using documents as evidence in a court of law, those documents need to have some weight to them, they need to have some reliability factors to them, and with this type of document there is none, respectfully, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you, perhaps, especially on the matter of whether this is all of it, that this is this part, or -- respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best if I ask the witness whether he recalls whether -- this entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, when you reviewed this, did you note that there was any portion of the conversations that you had with Mr. Mladic that was not included in these documents, recognising that they're not verbatim transcripts?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This brought to mind those conversations that I had in that year, in 1995, and as I -- as I recall them, they are -- represent what the conversation that took place on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome, any further information as to how they were created?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we go into private session for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber denies the objections raised. Madam Registrar, the numbers to be assigned to the two intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 27615 receives number P790; and document 27613 receives number P791, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P790 and P791 are admitted. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I now ask that 65 ter 3529 be brought to our screens. It is a letter purporting to be from General Smith to General Mladic, dated 26th June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And again, General, once you are able to see the document on your screen, can you tell us whether it is a document that you have reviewed recently, and if so, tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This is -- as it says, a letter from me to General Mladic, and I recognise it as the -- as one I looked at beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The introductory paragraph states: "I write further to the letter signed by my Chief of Staff on my behalf concerning Srebrenica. I wish to express my increasing concern about a sequence of very serious incidents." Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber in greater detail what it was you were attempting to communicate to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Throughout June, the enclaves, including Sarajevo, had come under increasing pressure, and this was particularly the case in the eastern enclaves: Zepa, Gorazde, and Srebrenica. The -- the precise incidents I don't recall, but there was an increasing crescendo of incidents or a crescendo was building up. The -- and I'm trying to get Mladic to understand that this the -- the safe area and the exclusion zones, which system, the exclusion zone system had already broken down as a result of what had happened in May, but that we were -- now the safe areas system was breaking down. We were not being able to feed the people inside them properly, and this was getting worse and worse, and I wanted to get this quite clearly laid out for him, at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 3529 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3529 becomes Exhibit P792, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Groome, to the extent there would be a better legible original, especially the lower part, apparently the translators have once had a copy which they could read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will investigate that, Your Honour. But let me, while the witness is here, take advantage of his presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He has said that this is a document he recognises and he has looked at, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was going to ask him whether you recognise anything missing or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The portion of the page which seems to be damaged, that's blacked, do you recall whether there's anything under there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it looks like the top of my signature. So apart from the -- something saying General Rupert Smith underneath it and possibly a -- a -- recording that a copy has gone to somebody, I don't expect to find anything else under there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will try to see if we can find a better copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now see P363. And if we go to page 7 in the original, and page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I would now like to move to that portion of your evidence which concerns July 1995. I would like to begin by asking you to you take a look at an entry from General Mladic's military notebook for 15 July. In this entry, General Mladic recorded a meeting in Dobanovci on 15 July 1995 and indicates that you were one of the attendees. Do you recall meeting Mladic on 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we advance to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The note from the meeting purports to record a conversation between you and General Mladic, in which he notes: "Treatment of the population in Srebrenica and Zepa. There are rumours" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have the right page in B/C/S on our screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In fact, Your Honour, could I ask that we use the actual photocopy of the diary of the notebook itself, if that's possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever, but the corresponding page. The original is fine if you have the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And page 7 in the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Handwritten version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- digital image handwritten version is -- is the e-court page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "There are rumours about atrocities, massacres, and rape" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we need is also an English version. So the handwritten version should replace the transcribed version, and then next to it I'd like to have English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: English is on page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being brought up, do you recall during this meeting on the 15th of July telling Mr. Mladic or discussing with him information you had regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will ask you to provide more detail about this meeting in a few minutes, but I would like to return to the days prior to the meeting so that the Chamber has an understanding of what information you had and the UN had prior to this meeting. In paragraphs 149 and 151, you state that you went on leave from the 1st of July and returned to BiH in the evening of the 12th. Do you recall what time you returned to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not so much to Bosnia but it was late in the evening. It was certainly dark. We were in the middle of summer, so it would have been late on the night of the 12th. And that was getting into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 149, you state that while you were away, you were accompanied by a radio operator to communicate with your command. Did you remain in contact with your command and receive briefings about the situation in Bosnia while you were on leave?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Once you returned on the 12th, were you briefed on developments in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 152, you summarise your assessment of the situation as follows: "Firstly, there was a major refugee problem, up to 35.000 refugees had already started to arrive in the Tuzla area. Secondly, I had to recover the Dutch Battalion. The whereabouts and fortunes of the Bosnian defenders of Srebrenica were unknown to me, although I was aware that captured men were being separated from the refugees and I had received reports of abductions and murders from the Bosnians but as yet these were unconfirmed." General, my question for you is whether you know the source of the information that you are provided with at this point in time, the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: From memory, the reporting that my briefing would have been taken -- would have been -- would have come from my staff and their reports from DutchBat in Srebrenica, although there were also reports going into Zagreb and to the -- to The Hague, to the capital, and they would have received informing from that direction as well, I suspect. In addition, the Bosnian government in Sarajevo were communicating with my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that 65 ter 3535 be now brought to our screens. It is a series of UN documents all from around the period of the massacres in Srebrenica. They were recovered from the UN archive by the OTP as a packet of material and some markings on the documents suggest they were transmitted as a single packet, and so I will preserve that characteristic of the exhibit as it may be relevant to the Chamber's consideration of them. There are seven documents in the packet, and I am able if the Chamber would be assisted to enumerate those documents now for the record, or I can just deal with them in turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it would be preferable that you deal with them in turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, your evidence with respect to the series -- this series of documents will be more easily understood if we examine them in chronological order of their creation rather than in the order in which they were assembled in this packet of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to e-court page 9 in the original, and 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first document is a report of a meeting you had with BiH Prime Minister Silajdzic on 13 July 1995. Have you had a chance to familiarize yourself with this and the other documents in this packet of materials?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, the first sentence of the report of the meeting states as follows: "General Smith met Prime Minister Silajdzic at the Presidency at 1420 hours on 13 July 1995. They discussed the current situation in Srebrenica, the refugee crisis, and unconfirmed reports of atrocities." Do you recall who raised the topic of the refugee crisis? Was it you or was it the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My memory is that I led on the refugee crisis, and -- because I wanted the -- the Bosnian government was trying to use this situation -- in their eyes the UN had failed and failed utterly, and that the UN should sort of the refugee problem that was a consequence of that failure. The -- however, we couldn't cope with that, unless the Bosnians played an active part in housing these people and so forth, and I was trying to get the prime minister's co-operation in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the prime minister provide you with additional information to that information you already possessed regarding the refugee crisis?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall a particular volume of information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who raised the reports of atrocities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think that would have been Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last sentence in paragraph 4 - and if we could advance to the next page of B/C/S - of the report states: "Thirdly, he requested the UN to provide medical and food aid and shelter to the refugees at Tuzla airport." Can you explain to the Chamber what was the refugee crisis at the Tuzla airport.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- the refugees were coming over the -- the entry point across the confrontation line, between the Bosnians and the Bosnian Serbs, was, if I recall, correctly, at Zvornik, and some way south of Tuzla. And the -- the only place where we had any area in which to move these refugees that was under UN control was Tuzla, and so we started to move the refugees there as they arrived. But there were no facilities for them there. They were in range of Serb artillery, and there was -- we had only a very limited amount of tents and cooking facilities and so forth with which to start building a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At this point in time, had anyone made the observation that able-bodied men were generally not among this group of refugees?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall it being made as specifically as you state it, but it was generally understood, yes, that these were women and children and old men that -- only.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention now to paragraph 152 of your statement. In particular, sentence 4, which begins: "By the end of July -- of 13 July, I believed there to have been a breakout by the defenders. In what numbers and with what success, I was not clear, and the ABiH were not telling me. We thought that some 2.000 male prisoners had been taken by the Bosnian Serbs and were being held in the vicinity of Bratunac." What was your source for this information, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically. The -- it would have been part of my briefings. It would have been a conversation which I think I had with the CO of the Dutch Battalion. And it would also have been me looking at the map and trying to understand the -- forming a picture of what had been happening on the information that I had available. A -- a defence doesn't collapse just like that without the defenders either being dead, and there was no evidence that they were, or captured, and we could only account for about 2.000 people, so where were the others? And my assumption, I suspect at that stage, is that they had broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we return 65 ter 3535 to the screens and that we go to the second document I would like to use. And that can be found at e-court page 11 in the original and 14 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, again, once you see the document, can you tell us, did you have an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. And I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell us what it is that you wrote; and can you orient us to the purpose and context of this document.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In situations such as this, it has been my habit as a commander to write out what I think the situation is and what the -- and what the options are that might present themselves and then to distribute this, if -- if it's suitable to do so, to my subordinates so that we all have a common picture of what the situation is and an idea of the priorities that I might be setting and the boundaries, if you like, of any future action. This, of course, gets updated as events unfold, but this was me doing this at the end of that day, in fact, the first day I'm back in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the Court Officer assist us by turning the document upside down and focussing on the bottom edge of the document. And, General, in preparation for your evidence today, did I ask you to study this marking and interpret it for us, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document should be turned. It's now upside down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I did want it to be upside down. There is a portion of text which is upside down which can be more easily read if the document is turned upside down. So could we turn the document upside down? And focus in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, are you able to interpret that text?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It only -- it's telling you that this was transmitted at 2331, whether that's local time or Greenwich Mean Time, I'm not sure, but I suspect it's local time, and on the 13th of July, and it's the -- the -- the accounting system, as it were, of the electronic machinery that's transmitting this copy, I imagine, to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the term BH command crypto?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It's my headquarters signals detachment, and it's their cryptographic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we turn the document right side up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, the Chamber will be able to read the document for themselves, but I want to draw your attention to two portions to ensure the Chamber has a full understanding of what you're communicating. First, can we look at paragraph 2(a). In this paragraph, you use the acronym RRF. Can you tell the Chamber what that acronym stands for?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This is the Rapid Reaction Force. And it begins as a -- as a force in the aftermath of the events at the end of May, where I form a -- a small element mainly based on -- in fact entirely based on the British and French detachments in Bosnia. The -- this finds favour with the -- specifically Britain and France and subsequently other troop-contributing nations and is reinforced. And during June, it becomes, if you like, an officially sanctioned reality, and other elements are supplied by France and Britain and ultimately the Netherlands, which are starting to deploy in June into -- and July, into the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the first sentence of paragraph 3 states: "The Bosnian Serbs are 'cleansing' Srebrenica." Cleansing is placed in quotation marks. Can you describe what your intent was by placing "cleansing" in quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it was a -- the word had become jargon in the theatre, which is probably why I put it in inverted commas, and it implies that the people in that place, which, in this case, is Srebrenica, are being driven out to some other destination, but the area is being cleaned of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The paragraph continues to describe unconfirmed reports of abductions and murders. Can I ask you to describe what was your understanding of the magnitude of any abductions or murders at this stage.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'd start by saying that these reports were, at this stage, in the main, coming from the Bosnians, and they would be saying that, wouldn't they? So I'm -- everything that's being told to me, I'm taking with a quite a lot of -- of salt at the time, wanting to see some evidence to support it. Secondly, we knew that this -- that the Bosnian Serbs practiced this ethnic cleansing, as it was called. We knew that people would be separated and that -- that's what happened in this war. And that -- and you do get in these circumstances incidents of people being killed and so forth. So with -- in a disaster such as the collapse of the defence of Srebrenica, I'm not surprised to find some incidents occurring and being reported. They're regrettable, they don't want to happen, and you don't went them to continue, but it wasn't a huge surprise to be hearing some of these reports, and I had no sense of -- of their magnitude at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can now go to the third document that I wish to work with. This can be found on 14 -- the original packet of documents and 18 in the translation. Can I now draw your attention to a report by Major Fortin dated 13 July 1995. This document reports on a meeting between VRS liaison, Lieutenant-Colonel Indic, and UNPROFOR representatives on 13th. If I can draw your attention, in particular, to paragraph 6. I believe we'll need to advance the page. It's on 15 and 19 respectively. It states: "Next, they discuss the return of stolen UNPROFOR weapons ..?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We wait a second until we have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that we go to the next page and see if the paragraph carries over. It should be 15 in e-court. So this is General Smith's letter. If we could move to the next document, please. I believe it follows immediately after this. And to the next page. I think we have it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third full paragraph on this page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In that paragraph we see: "Next they discussed the return of stolen UNPROFOR weapons. Lieutenant-Colonel [sic] Indic said they could let us inspect small arms to demonstrate that they were not used, but he could not return them without Mladic's approval." Can you comment on this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I wouldn't -- it doesn't surprise me. I -- I would have been very surprised if Indic was prepared to do anything without Mladic's approval. He was Mladic's liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, specifically, what weapons are being referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: These, I think, are the French weapons that had been taken in the aftermath of the bombing in -- in -- at the end of May and -- and had been used -- and in the -- when prisoners were taken at the Vrbanija bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now go to the next document. It is a public statement by Akashi on the 13th of July. And it can be found on page 17 and 21 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, the Chamber will be able to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I simply want to draw your attention to the last sentence in the second paragraph which reads: "In compliance with Resolution 1004, unanimously adopted last night by the United Nations Security Council, I demand that the Bosnian Serb civilian and military authorities immediately allow unimpeded access to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and other international agencies." Can you set out the reasons why it was so important for the UN to gain immediate unimpeded access to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at this stage, there were -- the bulk of the refugees were still in the vicinity of Srebrenica. They were not all across the border into Bosnian territory. Secondly, we didn't know what had happened to the rest of the population and how many casualties there were and so on. And until we got some access and got some idea of what was going on, we couldn't help anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What role, if any, did Mladic play in the UN's ability or inability to gain access throughout Srebrenica after this resolution was passed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
