utterances.text: I don't think he made any attempt to let anybody into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that we go to the first document in this packet. It can be found on e-court page 1 in both languages. And it is a code cable from Akashi to the Secretary-General dated 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak into the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you are kindly requested to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith I want to spend some significant amount time on this code cable and the reports attached to it and incorporate it into it. Have you had an opportunity to carefully review this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I have. I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last sentence on page 1 states: "An UNMO patrol into the town of Srebrenica reports that the town is deserted and BSA soldiers were looting the town. The report also touches on the rumours circulating among the DPs of maltreatment" of "the Bosnian Serb army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You take "by." You read "of."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it continues: "In view of the position of the UNMOs, we recommend that the source of any information released in this report be kept confidential." Can you explain that last portion of what I've read.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can. The UNMOs are not under my command, but -- and so exactly where these -- this UNMO team has come from, I'm not sure. They -- there was certainly an UNMO team or more than one in the Srebrenica area, and to the best of my knowledge, they were with the Dutch Battalion in Potocari. It -- it would seem that they had, in one way or another, been able to leave Potocari and -- and tour around the area, but they may have come from another direction, for all I know. The fact that they had been able to do this is, I suspect, why Mr. Akashi is saying that this -- their ability to collect this information should be kept confidential at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now turn to e-court page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are now five pages that appear very similar to this particular page. Can you tell us what is the document that we are now looking at?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This is the -- again, UNMO reporting in a daily situation report. And they're reporting these -- this particular, that, on the -- at 8.00 local time on the 13th, there's a medical convoy stopped at Kladanj, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to what appears as a subheading in the document, which states: "Srebrenica Update: DTG 130800B Jul 95." Can you interpret this for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes I can. DTG stands for date, time, group. The date is the 13th, the time is 0800 time zone Bravo, which is two hours plus of Greenwich mean time, in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was Bravo time the local time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I confirm my understanding of your evidence by asking would I be correct to conclude that the very next subheading pertains to an update from 1100 hours on the 13th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now under this second heading we read in the seconds sentence: "General Mladic gave assurances that the convoy was acceptable, so there should not be any problem with that convoy in Zvornik and at yellow bridge." What does this indicate to you about the level of Mr. Mladic's personal involvement at this stage?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, he is the one dealing with -- and here I'm making an assumption, the -- the UNMO team who's sending this update, and that he is the person that is in control of -- who comes and goes into the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to e-court page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, further down in this particular report, from 11.00 on the 13th, the report continues: "The number of BiH soldiers those are taken POW by the Bosnian Serb army is not known yet, but General Mladic told the UNMO team and the CO DutchBat that the BiH have several hundred dead soldiers in the area of the Bandera Triangle. He also asked the CO DutchBat to contact BiH soldiers and inform them that it is not the general's intention to kill any more soldiers of the BiH. They only have to surrender and hand over their weapons. The UNMO team and DutchBat are not allowed to enter that area because of safety, therefore can't investigate the numbers." Now my first question is: This report is from 11.00 in the morning of the 13th, and Mladic is recorded as having stated there are several hundred BiH soldiers dead in the Bandera Triangle. Do you recall at this point in time an area around Srebrenica that was referred to as the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know from where in the enclave a column did break out and head for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It -- my understanding at the time and is -- and is now is that the breakout occurred on the -- to the north-west of the enclave. In the general direction of the north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we look at P0038 on our screens?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that, Mr. Groome, we're close to the time where we'd take a break. Could you tell us where you are? We had a late start today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'm approximately halfway through my examination given the number of -- by just by looking at the number of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you asked for two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think that I will have to be revising that estimate upwards somewhat, Your Honour, given the importance of this witness's evidence. I might -- would be in a better position at the beginning of the next session to advise the Chamber how much I think additional time I would require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we first take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I perhaps just deal with this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a very small point I want to make with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can you please take a look at P38 on our screens. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what's the relationship between this document and the one we just looked at, the report we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think this is the source document, if you like, of the summary that's in the annex of the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are several headings at the top of that document. What is the significance of the heading: 13 July 1995 09:11:29?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm -- I need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just at the very, very top, and it looks like someone has hand-circled the original.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh right, it's there. That would be -- I don't know why it was circled. But it's -- it's the date it was sent and originated -- I'm sorry, date it was sent on -- at 9.11. And then this is the date, time, group, [indiscernible]. Yes. I'm not sure. I'm not sure I can tell you the significance of that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we can please take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome, you've used one hour and 40 minutes. Just as the Chamber yesterday easily agreed to the request of the Defence to -- not to sit extended hours and not to limit time in relation to what seems to be an important witness, the Chamber allows you to go beyond the time of your estimate, but there are certain limits there. If you could conclude in one hour and 30 minutes from now, that would give you almost double the time as have you used -- and -- the same time as you have used until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is much appreciated, and I have re-examined my examination, and I think there are some of these documents that perhaps I'll just rely on the tendering of them as associated exhibits. If I may continue, now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, before I leave P38, I just want to inquire whether perhaps over the break it had come to you whether can you help us in understanding that endorsement that has the circle around it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid it can't -- I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to assist the Chamber after having looked at the documents related to this report on the Bandera Triangle, to assist the Chamber in understanding the parameters of when that report was likely made recording Mladic's statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think it's being made quite early in the morning on the 13th. But I'm -- I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is that based on?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this -- we go back to this date, time, group at the top. The date, time, group, is, you've got is recorded as 1100 Bravo. That's on the -- on the -- you can see to and from, to TX from TA. I don't know what those are, but there's -- date, time, group there is 1100 Bravo on the 13th. But you've got another time listed at the one with the circle around it where it says 13th of July, and then the time there is at 9.00 in the morning -- yes, 9 hours, 11 minutes, 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And based on that you believe this report was made on the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. And it said the information in it is even earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now the Chamber has taken judicial notice in adjudicated facts 1530 and 1531 that the massacres of large numbers of men in Srebrenica commenced on the afternoon and evening of the 13th. If you assume for the purposes of my question that the Bandera Triangle was located in the west, south-west area of the enclave, is Mladic's statement recorded on the morning of the 13th, that hundreds of soldiers had been killed there, accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Just let me read that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm reading the question again. I will have to pose an objection as it calls for speculation. It assumes facts not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I can ask it another more direct way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase then your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, either at this time or any time after this, did you ever learn that hundreds of BiH soldiers had been killed in this west, south-west portion of the Srebrenica enclave at some point prior to the morning of the 13th?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't. It -- certainly not at stage. And you've said did I learn about it afterwards? I did learn that lots of people had been killed. The exact location of those killings, I don't recall at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now further down in paragraph 5 of this report we see the following sentence: "DutchBat are not allowed to enter that area," this is a reference again to Bandera Triangle, "because of our safety. We can't investigate the number." Do you know if the determination that it was too unsafe for DutchBat to move around the enclave was a decision taken by DutchBat or a restriction placed on their movement by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: My understanding at the time is they were being restricted in their movement by VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now ask that we go to page 7 in the original, and nine in the translation of this document, and to the subheading entitled: "Refugee Situation at Kladanj DTG-13 2300, July 1995." Now if I can draw your attention to the portion of that report which states: "The important point to note at the transfer point is there are no men over the age of 16, bar a few over 60." Would DutchBat have been the source of this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: At Kladanj, no. I wouldn't have thought they were the -- I mean, that wasn't part of their --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to assist us --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not actually -- hang on a minute. I would have to -- one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And tell us if you want to advance a page or go back a page?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I would like -- I don't mind -- go to back, if you see what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Go back one page?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think they're still looking -- are we still looking at an UNMO report?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could go to the first page in this document which is at e-court page 4 in both languages. So this is a series of five pages and this is now the first page that we're bringing to the screen.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- this is the annex to the UNMO daily sitrep. Now if we go back to the one you first showed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's page 7 in the original and 9 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And I think it -- this is UNMO reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would be -- are you able to say where the UNMOs would have been based?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know where those -- I just don't know at this stage. I might have known at the time, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3535 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness has discussed it as detailed, but it's based on a number of assumptions and I'm not quite sure between this document and the other document how much of this was known to the witness before reviewing these documents when presented by the Office of the Prosecutor. So on that bases, I would object to their admission as not being -- not being tied to the knowledge of this witness. Both this document and the one that we did prior, which has not been tendered yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is denied. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3535 receives number P793, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P793 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, now having looked at what information was known on the 13th and 14th of July, could I ask you to now return to your meeting with Mladic on the 15th. Before you describe the meeting and the substance of the meeting, can I ask you to, as it were, set the stage, give the Chamber some idea of the context, the format, the location of the meetings. Could you please do that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- from my point of view, this starts on the -- on the 14th with a request for me to get myself to Belgrade. We get out of Sarajevo. We go down to Split. We fly to Belgrade -- I beg your pardon. We fly to Zagreb. We fly to Belgrade. The meeting is the first time for a long time that I saw -- there was the -- the negotiating, political negotiating level of Carl Bildt; Stoltenberg; together with Akashi; General De La Presle; Stoltenberg's military advisor; the Force Commander, for -- everybody was in the same place, and the catalyst, if you like, of this event was the collapse of the Srebrenica safe area and the refugees. I don't think anybody understood what had actually happened there at this stage. The -- we start with a meeting amongst ourselves and then we move to meet Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When did you actually arrive at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I got there - let me think - I think about noon on the - what day would it be. The 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you arrived there had any meetings taken place before your arrival that you were made aware of?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I think that Carl Bildt had met with Milosevic and that -- all -- with the Akashi and I and the Force Commander, General Janvier, we had all arrived together. But I think the others had met beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe the first meeting you had upon your arrival. First let's start by can you describe who you met with. Name all the participants.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There was Stoltenberg, de La Presle, Janvier, Akashi, myself. I had a Colonel Baxter with me. General De La Presle had a Colonel Elliot with him. And I can't remember who was supporting the other principal actors.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you were asked to have a smaller meeting with Mr. Mladic himself?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. We all met at the hunting lodge, and very soon after we had all gathered around, and Mladic and Milosevic were there when we arrived. The -- it -- we -- we, General Mladic and I, were told to go away and sort out the, if you like, the modalities of Srebrenica in relation to the refugees and the extraction of the Dutch battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is of course is found in 157, to that extent repetitious. If you are short in time, would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where precisely was this particular meeting held?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In a room. The -- everyone else -- we had all met on a sort of patio outside the building. The, if you like, the military members, General Mladic and I, we went to some anteroom actually in the building, and the remainder of the meeting stayed on the patio.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 162 of your statement you say quote, referring to Mladic: "He warned me that his troops in the Gorazde area were awaiting his orders to attack and claimed a significant victory in the Treskavica mountains near Sarajevo." Was it your understanding that he was presently and actively giving orders to his subordinates while at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did he say or do anything which indicated to you that he had given another person temporary direct authority to issue orders while he attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think he ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you consider that you yourself, while at that meeting, were in actual command of the troops under your command?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now please return to P363, General Mladic's military notebook, and if we could go, once again, to 7 in the digit image of the notebook, and 4 in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being brought up, General Mladic records you as saying three things, and I want to put them to you and ask you to explain. If we could go, I'm sorry, to the next page, please, in both. And once again, if we could please call up the digital image of the actual notebook. While that is being down I will read the text and you can confirm it when you see it on the screen. The first thing he records you as saying is: "I will use the force when the UN forces come under attack on the road or at the camp." Do you recall saying something along these lines to Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, with respect to the -- I'm sorry. If I could just get the right English page up here. With respect to the English, it should be page 5 in the English, in e-court. I think that's it there now. Okay. So now we have it. Okay. I'm sorry, I interrupted you. Can you please --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The forces I think I was referring to is -- is the air force, the -- the -- you know, use air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what's the camp that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I suspect the camp at Gorazde, if that was the -- it -- it -- I don't remember the connection, but if we are talking about a threat to the British battalion or the Ukrainian forces in Gorazde, then it would have been if their camp was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next note records you as saying: "Treatment of the population in Srebrenica and Zepa - there are rumours about an atrocities, massacres, and rape."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think we should have the corresponding page in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we advance the original copy one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General Smith, my question to you is do you say -- do you recall saying something along those lines to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you used the word "rumours"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember that specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last note in this notebook entry, and if we could advance the translation at this stage, regarding you as: "It would be good if you would allow the UNHCR and International Committee of the Red Cross as soon as possible." Do you recall saying something along these lines?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to get access. We're -- we, that is, I, the UNHCR, and the ICRC, are still looking for what we think are some 2.000 prisoners of war plus, and we don't know how many the plus is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now please go to 01935. It's 65 ter number. Now, during the course of this meeting with Mladic, did you begin to develop a draft agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, 65 ter 1935 is on the screen. Did you have a chance to review this document before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the substance that's discussed or written in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And Your Honours so the Court has some understanding, this is also a document recovered with one of the notebooks. Item number 3 indicates that representatives of the UNHCR will be allowed to enter Srebrenica by 18 July 1995 at the latest. Did Mladic explain why he would not agree to immediate access?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: To the best of my memory, the -- this was all to do with the security of people and that they were -- you know, there were still Bosnian soldiers about that my be creating incidents and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 1935 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to this document being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1935 becomes Exhibit P794, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now could I ask that we please bring to the screen 65 ter 5729. This is a document dated 19 July 1995 from Lieutenant-Colonel Baxter and entitled: "Meeting, General Smith, General Mladic, 19 July 1995." My first question to you is: Do you recall meeting, again, with General Mladic on the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to page 3 in the original and 4 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in paragraph 3(c) it states: "General Smith explained that it was particularly important for UNHCR to have immediate access to Srebrenica in order to assess requirement for future aid convoys. Mladic agreed to this without difficulty." My question to you is: When would be the first time UNHCR would gain access to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find that bit on the paper [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's 3(c). If you look at the very top there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't see anything where I'm saying about access. In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "It seems that in the discussion General Smith explained that it was particularly important" -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, got you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. The -- I don't think UNHCR ever got access in the end to the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mladic ever give an explanation as to why they were not given access?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not in my memory, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last sentence on the original, and if we could advance to page 5 in the B/C/S, states with the word "he," referring to Mladic: "He said he engaged himself personally in this operation and organised as much food and water for the refugees as possible." My question to you is: Do you recall General Mladic stating that he had been personally involved in VRS operations in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. It misstates the document, Your Honour. It's testifying and it misstates the document and calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, let me have -- you were quoting exactly from -- let me see where it is on the -- on the top, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The bottom of page 2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you understand this language to be that he took part or that -- let me ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and that was my next question with the witness to clarify his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He only talks about the organisation of food and water for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not this operation. Witness, where it reads here that Mr. Mladic would have said that he engaged himself personally in this operation, which is described to you a minute ago, and organised as much food and water for the refugees as possible, how did you -- how do you interpret this language? Is that Mr. Mladic was exclusively engaged in this operation, as far as food and water is concerned, or whether it was to be understood in a wider sense, and, if so, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood it on the wider basis, that he was engaged personally on this operation, and indeed I'd seen television footage of him being engaged personally on this operation in the streets of Srebrenica and around Potocari. So that was my understanding at the time, and -- and that is how I continued to read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now go to paragraph 5. This can be found on 4 in the original, and page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The portion I want to draw your attention says: "Mladic described how on the night of 10/11 July 1995, a significant number of BiH troops broke through the lines in the direction of Tuzla. He explained that he had opened a corridor to let these troops go. He accepted that some skirmishes had taken place with casualties on both sides and that some 'unfortunate small incidents' had occurred." That's the end of the quote of that. My question to you is: What did you understand him to mean when he said "unfortunate small incidents"?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It would have been things like people trying to surrender, getting shot, people -- people who weren't armed being shot. Those sorts of things. Which I can envisage happening in those sorts of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 5729 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5729 becomes Exhibit P795, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P795 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now go to 65 ter 5733. And this is notes on a meeting between Generals Smith and Mladic on 31st of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, did there come a time when you met General Mladic on the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there anything memorable about your travel to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, my helicopter was shot up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it hit?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was your helicopter shot on the way to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was -- it was engaged on our way to the meeting as we crossed from Bosnian-held bits of Sarajevo and into the Bosnian Serb area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the outer markings of the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was a UN marked helicopter of the British Sea King, it was the type of helicopter, with UN markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was your trip announced to both sides.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you travelling in daylight?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was in daylight and it wasn't so much as announced. We had been given clearance for this meeting and this journey by Mladic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to paragraph 8 and that can be found on the third page in both languages, which is entitled: "UNHCR Aid to Sarajevo." The last sentence of this paragraph summarising the discussions related to Sarajevo states, referring to Mladic: "He then offered to take measures to open Sarajevo airport and return all Sarajevo utilities if UNPROFOR removes the BiH from the Igman DMZ, suggesting that we had the forces in place to do this." Did you understand during the course of this meeting for Mladic to represent that he had the personal capacity to control the inflow of utilities into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It -- it -- and the -- the -- this offer is indicative of it, but it is also that if I'd agreed to that, I was assuming, which was not a safe assumption, that the Bosnians would permit me to, in fact, shot down the Igman trail, he would then be entirely in control of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if I draw your attention to a meeting on the 22nd of August 1995 and ask you to take a look at paragraph 194 of your statement, and this is P785, MFI, page 49 and 38 respectively. It says: "Later in the meeting, I tackled Mladic on Srebrenica and the allegations of atrocities. It was clear by now that these massacres had taken place." Can you explain this portion of your meeting with as much precision as possible, including what you said to Mladic and he to you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- just let me, for a moment, just refresh my memory of the earlier paragraphs in that statement. Yeah. During this meeting, I'm trying to explain the -- the political situation, the international political situation and the progress of the -- what had come to be called the Holbrooke peace talks. And trying to get him to understand, the -- that the -- that repeatedly the Bosnian Serbs had put themselves into positions where their -- the impression they gave was so revolting to public opinion, that their position, their argument that they were trying to advance was being dismissed before they'd been able to make their argument because of their actions as seen on television and so forth. And I'm trying to get that across at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd like to change to a different subject now. In paragraphs 189 to 210 of your statement concerns events in August 1995 and includes the shelling on the market-place in Sarajevo on 28 August. Your evidence is comprehensive on this point. I do want to draw your attention to paragraph 201. That can be found on page 51 and 40 respectively in e-court. In your statement, you say: "There was an acoustic system called HALO that didn't pick up any firing from within the city, which told us that it was out of range of acoustic system." Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber what is H-A-L-O or HALO and explain it in the context of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: HALO was an acoustic target acquisition system. It has a number of sensors. The -- it -- a weapon is fired. It hears the firing of the weapon. The sensors all produce a direction and you -- you -- each one is compared to the other -- excuse me, one minute. And then you can begin to get a direction of where the weapon was fired from. In addition to this form of information, and as said in this paragraph, there is the Cymbeline radar, and then finally you had the observation posts around the confrontation line of -- in Sarajevo and they, too, are part of your acoustic system in that the people can hear a weapon being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that 10244 be brought to our screens. It is a document entitled "Final and Comprehensive Report on the 28 August 1995 Mortar Incident," dated 8 September 1995. Once it's on the screen, I'd ask you whether you have had a chance to examine this document in preparation for your evidence today.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us what it is we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- this is a collection of documents put together by my military assistant and as to the background to our understanding and how we reached our understanding of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 10244 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection to the tendering of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, is it correct that you did not tender 65 ter 5733?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I may not have, Your Honour. I apologise and thank you for the reminder. It is my intention to tender that document, Your Honour, and I would do so at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 5733. No objection to the document being tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 5733 would receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P796 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P796 is admitted. Then we have 65 ter 10244.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P797 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next three -- well, let me ask General Smith something first.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After the Markale bombing, you had a number of phone calls with General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter, and the core number -- is the root number is the same for all the suffix differs, 22270M suffix P and suffix S are tape recordings of phone calls -- of these phone calls made by General Mladic and they were recovered from him. I asked Mr. Ivetic to consider whether he would consent to their admission, and if he makes his position known, perhaps I can save some time and not have the general look at them here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could have a minute to consult with my client on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you want to take instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's being done, could I ask that a document be brought to our screen, and it's 3548. And in fact, Your Honour, as I see Mr. Ivetic is coming back, perhaps he can make his position known and I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My client has instructed that he does not object to the admission of these documents so long as they are read and presented in their entirety so that the public gets the true, full picture of what was discussed and we get to the truth of the matters that are of interest to these proceedings finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Access of the public to these proceedings is a matter the Chamber will deal with. I do understand that Mr. Mladic does not object to their admission, and we'll take care that the public is informed as it usually is. Madam Registrar, 22270, and -- suffix P.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 22270M, first, will receive number P798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P798 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Mladic, no talking allowed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22270P receives number P799, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there the third one is the suffix S?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And document 22270S receives number P800, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P800 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I did have to consult with my colleague about the additional instructions to reiterate that Mr. Mladic expects that these are to be read or heard in their entirety in the courtroom. And in so as far there are audio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I not allowed to make a record, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I not allowed to make a record, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you please calm down, Mr. Ivetic. And, well, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I allowed to continue making my record, Your Honour, of what my client has instructed me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are interrupted by me at this moment and you have to accept that because I wanted to say something first, and then I will allow you to complete what you intended to say. What I wanted to say is that it may be clear to you that an objection to admission cannot be conditional. The Chamber does not accept conditions before it admits something. The Chamber understands the condition Mr. Mladic intended to impose as an expression of concern for the public character of this trial. That is a matter the Chamber will look at seriously, as it always does. That is what I wanted to say. If you now want to complete what you said, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And first I thank you for your comments and your understanding. Mr. Mladic also wanted to bring to the attention of the Chamber, as I understand it, that these are apparently from dictaphone cassettes which should be in the possession of the Prosecution and which can be played and can be heard, so we would ask that those cassettes be also entered into evidence, not just the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic -- Mr. Groome, are there any cassettes which could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have them prepared and they are here in court. That was our full intention to tender them as public exhibits, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the cassettes, the audio is part of the -- is it already? If not, is it uploaded?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm informed that the digital audio has already been transferred over to the Registrar and the transcripts have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take care that they are part of the record of these proceedings so it's not only text but also audio. Madam Registrar, how are we going to deal with that technically? Do we have to add something to the e-court records?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. This is standard procedure. I have been provided with copies and DVDs, the Chamber staff was provided with copies as well, and transcripts are uploaded in the e-court as I can see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, Mr. Ivetic, everything is part of the record now, including audio. And I think we could then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear, what's been transmitted to the Chamber has not been edited in any way by the Prosecution. It is the entire content of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, do you recall if during these conversations General Mladic was proposing that a joint commission be established to investigate the second Markale bombing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, he did propose this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In due course the Prosecution will adduce evidence about that these recordings were recovered from General Mladic. My question to you, at this point, when the conversation took place, were you aware that he was recording your conversation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask -- Your Honour, the next exhibit I want to work with is 3548. I only intend to tender the last two pages, pages 9 and 10, and have taken the liberty of creating a sub-exhibit, 3548A. If the Chamber permits, I will use that instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first ask Mr. Ivetic whether there's any objection against using two pages only of this document as a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not have an objection to the entire exhibit coming in. I don't have it in front of me right now to give an immediate response as to extract of. Since there are many documents that were disclosed for this witness, I don't have them at instantaneous recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest the following, that we follow the suggestion by Mr. Groome, and if you want the entire exhibit, the entire original exhibit to be in evidence, Mr. Ivetic, that we hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be appreciated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, sub-Exhibit 3548A is the one you want to work with at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that's what is on the screen now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, did you have a chance to review this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This is a -- an account of the conversations I had with Mladic, those -- on those two days, the 28th and 29th.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The entry in the middle of the page for 1823 hours on the 28th, it's reported that Mladic claimed that an examination of the casualty list and the circumstances of the incident would provide the truth and vindicate his forces. Did he explain to you how the identity of the victims would vindicate the involvement of his forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 3548A as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With reference to what I said earlier, Madam Registrar, this exhibit would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3548A receives number P801, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my final line of questioning should only be a few minutes. Could I ask that 65 ter 17494 be brought to our screens. It is an order from Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of the republic, strictly confidential number 1538-2/95, dated 26 March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Smith, have you had an opportunity to familiarise yourself with this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not as interested in the substance of the document as the procedure that was followed. But can I ask you to briefly summarise your understanding of this order issued by President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It's an order issued in -- on 26th of March, ordering the mobilisation of the state of -- of Republika Srpska, and the -- it -- it -- and it's all the organs of the state. This isn't just military. It's making sure that the whole of the state's effort is devoted to the -- to -- to the purpose of the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please now see 65 ter 7661.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's an order from the Main Staff dated the same date and type-signed by General Ratko Mladic. And, again, General, once you can see this document, can you tell us whether you have recently familiarised yourself with it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise its purpose in military terms.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is the military chain of command taking the political --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will interject and object to this opinion testimony coming in. The witness has not been qualified as an expert witness, and in fact has been disqualified on the topic of being an expert witness by other Trial Chamber as to the VRS. He can talk in general terms but he cannot apply his facts and conclusions specifically to the VRS. This has never been presented as an expert under 94 bis. This is constantly happening, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you finished, Mr. Ivetic? Mr. Groome, would you please rephrase the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply asking the witness, who has 40 years of a military officer and his experience as a commander of a multinational force, if he recognises what the purpose of this document would be. I'm not asking him to express any opinion about the effectiveness of a chain of command or anything like that, but simply what would be the purpose of such a document. I believe that's well within his realm of personal and professional experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. We'll then -- and the witness is invited not to avoid from any speculation and just to base his answer on experience preferably well explained so that the Chamber understands exactly what the basis for your comments is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we go back to the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's the one signed by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please have once again on the screen 17494.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. We can see in the original that there -- there is a strictly confidential number. It starts 01 in the top left-hand corner. And the next order, the one -- if we could down the chain, as it were, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please now have 7661.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you're asking us to note the --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That number at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now please see 7661.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And you now see the Main Staff of the army referring to this order in the second paragraph, "we received this strictly confidential order number," et cetera, the same number as the previous one, and we then see the order being repeated. And if it turns over the page, will probably tell you to obey it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's only one page in the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we now look at 65 ter 13045. This is a document dated the next day, 27 March 1995, from the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, again, once you can see it, have you recently familiarised yourself with this document?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And I'd only point out that the -- well, let me look at it. And there, again, at the -- in -- on my screen, the paragraph at the bottom of the page: "We've received an order from the RS president ... number 01," et cetera. And it repeats it and passes it on down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Finally can we look at 65 ter 13035.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's a document of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade dated 29 March, 1995, entitled in part: "Delivery of the Order of the President of Republika Srpska." Again, when can you see it, have you recently familiarised yourself with it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And here we see the subordinate formation of the Drina Corps commander repeating the order number that begins with 01 and repeating the order to their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally can we go to the last page in the English translation, the last sentence of the document which states: "The battalion commands are duty-bound to make known the contents of the order of the president of the republic through their company commanders to every soldier an officer so that they may be informed and acquainted with the application of regulations during a state of war ..." and it continues. Do you have any observations about that last sentence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Other than the -- that there is this -- if you like, there's the threat of punishment if you don't understand these orders and carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I tender these documents, I want to point out something with respect to 7661 and 13045. The English translation of 7661 records the VRS document number as 3/4-480. In 13045, which refers to this document, records the number as 03/4-490. It is the Prosecution's case that given the poor quality of the original identified as 7661, the translator has understandably misread the number 490 as 480. Since the original is illegible, I think asking for the translation to be verified will not resolve the matter but, rather, it will be for the Chamber to ultimately consider the related documents and come to its own view about what the real reference number is in fact. And with that, Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 17494, 7661, 65 ter 13045, 65 ter 13035 as public Prosecution Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence would object. I have heard no testimony from this witness giving any personal factual knowledge of either the matters contained in these documents or of having received the documents during the relevant time-period. What we've had here is trying to get an opinion testimony through the backdoor through a witness who has not had any personal knowledge to gain as to these documents and therefore we would object to the introduction of these three documents on this basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would there be any objection against having them admitted through the bar table because what the Prosecution apparently wants to establish, and almost everyone can read in those documents, is that an order is going down the line of the hierarchical military line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When they make a submission via the bar table we will examine it and we will give our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, would you extend the tendering to alternatively tendering them from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask Madam Registrar to mark them for identification, and we'd like to hear from you, Mr. Ivetic, well, let's say still this week. Madam Registrar, can you please assign numbers to the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17494 receives number P802, Your Honours. Document 07661 receives number P803, Your Honours. Document 13045 receives number P804, Your Honours. And document 13035 receives number P805, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. P802 up to P805, because the last one is missing on the transcript, but I think it was 13035 which receives exhibit number P805. Therefore, P802 up to and including P805 are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, General Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. We take another break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you are supposed not to speak aloud once the Chamber has entered the courtroom, which it has done by now. I would like to have, Mr. Ivetic, at the end of this session, seven minutes to deliver some guidance. Meanwhile, can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Groome, I already can announce what I'll read at the end of this session. That is, a statement regarding the Rule 94 bis filing of expert report of Witness Theunens. It could be that you want someone else to listen in as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I wish to take the opportunity to remind you that in so far as we both will be speaking the English language, we need to ensure that there is a pause between my question and your answer to allow for the interpretation to complete and, thus, make the job of the court reporter easier. Is that fair and understood, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would begin by focussing just briefly on your career and education and training. I would like now to move to the time-period before you were deployed to the former Yugoslavia. First of all, in your years of training and education to become a member of the British armed forces, did you ever have a course of study with a focus on the structure or doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army or the Yugoslav All People's Defence system?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not a specific course, no. But in my general training, the -- the structure of the -- the -- in the Yugoslavian army was addressed, but only in fairly general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Yugoslavian army. Can I ask you now to focus with regard to the Army of the Republika Srpska, the Armija BiH, or the Croat Defence Union. Did any of your study or training to become a member and officer of the British armed forces involve courses or relative to the structure or doctrine of these entities?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not in my -- not in the -- it wasn't -- it wasn't part of one's basic training, no. But in the job I did before I was deployed to Bosnia, I began to learn how these organisations were operating. But it wasn't a course of instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer that you began to learn that this was an independent study on your own part rather than a formal part of your employment?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, it was my job. We were -- we were sending people to these places, and I needed to understand what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what was the precise nature of your activities to begin to learn how these organisations were operating?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I was the assistant chief for the Defence Staff for operations and security in the Ministry of Defence in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On what sources did you rely to begin to learn how these organisations were operating?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: On the reporting that we were receiving, at that time, from the people we'd had deployed there and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were you able to, at the time of your deployment, speak the local language or any of the local languages of the former Yugoslavia, or did you always rely upon an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I couldn't speak, and don't speak, any of those languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please provide us with some details relating to the time when you were deployed as a member of UNPROFOR? Did you at that time receive any specific training, instruction, or briefing as to the operation function of the army BiH, Army of Republika Srpska, or the Croat Defence Union?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I was briefed by the headquarters when I took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did such a briefing take place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The initial one was probably about an hour and a half but this was a continuous process. It wasn't just a one -- one event.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any part of your briefing deal substantively with the locations of military storage facilities and military formations of the armija BiH within and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If you -- by that you mean the Weapons Collection Points and so forth, yes. In so far as we knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct that the briefings were only related to the Weapons Collection Points and not any suspected unreported caches of weapons and/or munitions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall there being an unreported or suspected cache, but if there had been I would expect I would have been briefed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to go into some more details about your career before you assumed command of UNPROFOR BH command in January of 1995. I'm looking at your statement, which is P785, marked for identification, and paragraph 4 of the same, which would be in page 2 of the English, and page 2 of the B/C/S as well. And I think you've already identified the position. The period I'm focussing on is from 1992 to 1993 when you served as the assistant chief of the UK Defence Staff for operations and security. And did you, as part of that entity within the Ministry of Defence of the United Kingdom, as part of your duties plan or assist in activities relating to covert British assets operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether as part of UNPROFOR or NATO or stand alone?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In my -- the covert operations would not have been conducted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now can I get an answer to my question. Did you plan or assist in any form the operations of covert British assets in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I was operating as a British officer and now I'm here as a UN officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're here as a witness of the truth, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. In which case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I would rather I didn't answer that question without some advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're supposed to answer questions that are put to you here. You're under a duty to testify. There's no Rule 70 restriction, Mr. Groome, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour. Could I ask that the questions be deferred to tomorrow so I can have an opportunity to review the Rule 70 paperwork on this. But I believe that this witness is here pursuant to Rule 70. This witness has testified here many many times, so there's -- if I could just have till the morning to review that paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'll be given time until tomorrow. And, Mr. Ivetic, could you then proceed at this moment and then we'll revisit this matter tomorrow, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a document in e-court about some of the work you were behind while at this Ministry of Defence position as the assistant chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Toward that end I would call up 65 ter number 25916 which is a transcript of the 12 January 2000 interview which you gave to the Dutch authorities, and I think the selection I want is at page 8, paragraph 30, of the same. I believe the English is page 8 and paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's no English version visible in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any Dutch version of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I thought we had an English version but [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently you have not. Well, then you have both something to consider before it is tomorrow, Mr. Ivetic. If by tomorrow if you could also find out whether there's an original Dutch version of this document, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My recollection is that there is a Dutch version. The English version was the question mark that I had. This is a Prosecution document, of course, but I do believe that I have seen a Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be appreciated if that would become part of e-court as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will skip this and we'll get back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, focussing on that time-period of 1993, was the British Ministry of Defence already at that time making plans to engage either by air-strikes or by artillery in combat actions against the Bosnian Serbs, and, if so, could you tell me if it was within the auspices of NATO or the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The British Ministry of Defence was not making those plans, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the British Ministry of Defence participating with others who were making those plans?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They -- the UN, at one stage, had a -- an element, an artillery element, held offshore in 1993, I think it was, and subsequently NATO established the no-fly zone, and after the no-fly zone the safe areas, and that involved the prospect or use of air power.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say that there was an artillery element held offshore. Am I correct that we're talking about British artillery pieces there on boats?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: On a ship, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I also correct, sir, that at that time in 1993 it was your personal proposal and position these artillery pieces should be brought onto the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina to be used against the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, it wasn't to be used against the Bosnian Serbs. And it was my personal opinion that our battle group should have that capability. But it was in defence of our people, rather than to act against anybody, unless they attacked us. It was also in response to the Bosnian Serbs shelling a British position, somewhere in the south. I can't remember the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you came into conflict or confrontation with your superiors about your will to use force against the Serbs at this time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. They agreed and we put the guns on the ships. The UN didn't want them in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you never came into confrontation with your superiors about your will to use force?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not in those terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. With regard -- with regard to the decision not to bring the British artillery on the ground and have it potentially used, am I correct that you were upset about this decision by your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall being upset about it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that in 1993 and 1994 whilst at the Ministry of Defence in London, you were already, at that time, involved in discussions between NATO headquarters in Brussels and the UN headquarters in New York regarding the use of NATO air-strikes in Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't working. I was the -- the British representative in these discussions in both headquarters. I wasn't co-ordinating between the UN and the NATO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I said I would need seven minutes. We have [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I defer to you, Your Honours. You can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Smith, there's not much chance that we would conclude your testimony tomorrow, so we were informed that you would still be available on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would need to make a couple of telephone calls to be absolutely sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then Mr. Groome informed us not completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I said with difficulty. I mean, he's being very co-operative, but it wasn't without difficulty so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We tried, Mr. Smith, to see whether we could conclude your testimony this week. Unfortunately we were unable and we would not like to cut the parties down on your testimony, which I hope you will understand as well. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. But I'd first like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether given already today or still to be given tomorrow or any other day to follow. If, in relation to the matter Mr. Groome will further explore what we call Rule 70; that is, confidentiality, if that raises a matter, and if you, as you said, you would have to consult someone, you first need the approval of the Chamber for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to deliver the Chamber's statement regarding Rule 94 bis filing of expert report of Witness Theunens. The Prosecution filed its notice of disclosure of expert report of Reynaud Theunens, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, on the 8th of January of this year, informing the Chamber of the disclosure of Theunens' expert report to the Defence on the 5th of October, 2012. According to the Prosecution, the report provides for an expert military analysis of the documentary evidence related to the existence and the purpose of the overarching joint criminal enterprise alleged in the indictment. At the outset, the Chamber notes that the current English version available in e-court under 65 ter number 28612 seems to have various pages in disorders. For example, page 184 of the document in e-court seems to be parts of a table of contents, followed by page 185, which is normal text again. This mix between table of contents pages and usual page -- usual text pages continues for about 19 pages. Similarly, page 213 of the document in e-court seems to be a cover page, then followed by a page that continues the text, which started on page 212. There are a manifold of other examples in the current version on the e-court. The Chamber expected the Prosecution to upload a proper version of the report. As this was not done, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to correct such mistakes when it uploads a new version and to inform the Defence and Chamber once it has done so. Further, the Chamber notes that "Part I: Background of the Report," comprises of a section covering three subsections that give a general summary of the SFRY armed forces, its military laws, and the conflict in Croatia between 1991 and 1992. The section in total amounts to 180 pages of the 686-pages-long document. In light of the substance covered by these pages, the Chamber expects the Prosecution to clearly explain the relevance of this section of the report. Part II of the report discusses the time-frame from 1992 to 1995. In this regard, the Chamber noted various areas of overlap between the report and the adjudicated facts in this trial. A couple of examples would be: The proclamation of the Serb Autonomous Districts, (report page 294), covered by adjudicated fact 56; the fact that the VRS could rely on personnel and equipment by the JNA (report page 334), covered by adjudicated facts 303; the declaration for a general mobilisation by the Bosnian Serb Presidency (report page 340), covered by adjudicated fact 306; or the proclamation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of BiH (report page 301), covered by adjudicated fact 128, to only name a few. The Chamber reminds the Prosecution that it insists on no, or a minimum of overlap of tendering of evidence, and, therefore, asks the Prosecution to properly review the report again and to redact any overlap with adjudicated facts in this case. In light of the above, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to take the steps outlined above and make a new filing, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules. And this concludes the Chamber's statement. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Friday, the 25th of January, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, III.
